note: Rewritten to the claim that survived the four independent audits.

problems.original_statement: Identification is a property of the observed data together with the assumptions, not a property of the estimator. A neural network cannot learn a counterfactual contrast that the data and assumptions do not identify, and flexible modeling that reduces approximation error in a nuisance function can at the same time disguise unsupported extrapolation, because a smooth fit extends confidently into regions with no observations. The distinction is stated clearly in the methodological literature and is repeatedly elided in applied work, where a more flexible learner is offered as the answer to a confounding or positivity concern. There is no diagnostic in common use that separates a flexible model interpolating where data exist from the same model extrapolating where they do not.
problems.correction_note: Support and overlap diagnostics that flag particular forms of extrapolation do exist, so the claim that no diagnostic separates interpolation from extrapolation was too strong. They are definition-dependent and model-dependent, and they cannot certify sequential exchangeability, positivity or identification, which is the weaker and correct version.
problems.statement: Identification is a property of the observed data together with the assumptions, not of the estimator. A flexible learner reduces approximation error in a nuisance function and cannot repair nonidentification, and the same smoothness that reduces that error extends the fit confidently into regions holding no observations. Support and overlap diagnostics can flag particular forms of extrapolation, and they depend on how support is defined and on the model producing them, so a passing diagnostic certifies nothing about sequential exchangeability, positivity or identification. The gap widens with high-dimensional treatment histories, where the region a prediction is being asked about is itself hard to characterize, and applied work continues to offer a more flexible learner as the response to a confounding or positivity concern.
problems.why_open: Extrapolation is invisible in any conventional fit statistic: a model can have excellent cross-validated loss on the observed region and be entirely unconstrained off it. The regions that matter are conditional on a growing treatment and covariate history, so whether a given prediction is supported is itself a high-dimensional question, and any diagnostic answering it has to define support in a way that is a modeling choice rather than a fact. The professional incentive also points one way, since the flexible estimate is the one with the tighter interval.
problems.proposed_direction: Pair every flexible nuisance model with a support diagnostic reported for the conditioning sets the model actually uses, and state the support definition, since the diagnostic is only as meaningful as that definition. Score estimators on failure awareness: whether their diagnostics signal a severe positivity violation or a non-identifiable target, tested against deliberately non-identifiable simulation scenarios. Include at least one such scenario in every methods comparison, because an estimator that always returns a narrow interval is not robust if it never warns.

problems.original_statement: Systems now translate trial descriptions into cohort definitions or analysis code, and natural language processing extracts eligibility information from unstructured notes. The failure mode of these systems is not that they crash. It is that they silently substitute a different estimand: mistranslating a temporal condition, resolving an ambiguous eligibility phrase to the wrong operationalization, or emitting code that is syntactically valid and causally invalid. None of these failures is visible in the output, which is a working pipeline returning a plausible number. What is missing is a validation regime that treats generated code as an untrusted artifact rather than as a productivity gain.
problems.correction_note: The entry argued that validation is impossible because the correct cohort is what the pipeline was built to produce. That is too strong: semantic fidelity can be tested against independently specified protocols, expert annotations, reference implementations and synthetic temporal boundary cases even when a gold-standard cohort for the real dataset is unavailable.
problems.statement: Systems now translate trial descriptions into cohort definitions or analysis code, and natural language processing extracts eligibility information from unstructured notes. The failure mode is not that they crash. It is that validly executing code implements a different estimand: a mistranslated temporal condition, an ambiguous eligibility phrase resolved to the wrong operationalization, a join that reads treatment before eligibility as treatment after it. None of that is visible in the output, which is a working pipeline returning a plausible number, and downstream numerical plausibility does not validate the translation. Semantic fidelity is testable, against independently specified protocols, expert annotations, reference implementations and synthetic patients built so each temporal condition has a case that distinguishes the correct reading from the plausible wrong one. No such regime is required or routine, and the artifact under review remains the number rather than the specification.
problems.why_open: Temporal logic is where these systems fail and where testing is hardest: the difference between treatment before eligibility assessment and treatment after it is one word in the specification and one join condition in the code, and both execute. A gold-standard cohort for a real dataset is often unavailable, which removes the most direct test and leaves the indirect ones, each of which costs the effort the automation was adopted to save. The systems are also spreading faster than any validation convention, now reaching concept-set authoring as well as protocol translation.
problems.proposed_direction: Treat automation as a constrained compiler: a human-authored causal specification, a typed intermediate representation, and data-source-specific code generated from it, with temporal-logic validation applied to the intermediate representation rather than to the output. Require unit tests over synthetic patients constructed so that each temporal condition has a case distinguishing the correct reading from the plausible wrong one, and test semantic fidelity against independently specified protocols and reference implementations where they exist. Require dual human sign-off on the specification and the generated cohort counts, and publish both, so what is reviewed is the specification and not the estimate.

problems.original_statement: Notes, imaging and device data capture severity, treatment rationale and outcomes that structured fields miss, and natural language processing has been proposed for eligibility extraction and phenotyping on that basis. The risk is specific: a learned representation of a clinical note is a dense summary of everything in the note, which can include post-treatment information, the identity of the site, the behavior of the treating clinician and protected characteristics. Adjusting for such a representation is adjusting for an object whose causal role is unknown and probably mixed, and the usual justification, that more information reduces confounding, does not hold when part of that information is a descendant of treatment.
problems.correction_note: Two corrections. A timestamp preceding assignment is not sufficient: what matters is that the input window is demonstrably prior to both the assignment and the underlying treatment decision, which is a provenance requirement rather than a date check. And the entry's proposed test, whether the embedding predicts treatment better than structured covariates do, neither establishes nor rules out leakage. Formal treatment-leakage methods and text distillation exist without being standard.
problems.statement: Notes, imaging and device data capture severity, treatment rationale and outcomes that structured fields miss, and natural language processing has been proposed for eligibility extraction and phenotyping on that basis. A learned representation of a clinical note is a dense summary of everything in the note, which can include the site, the treating clinician's behavior, protected characteristics and information about a treatment decision already made. An embedding whose input window is not demonstrably prior to both the assignment and the decision behind it can therefore carry post-treatment content into a nominal baseline adjustment set, and a timestamp preceding assignment does not establish that it does not. Formal treatment-leakage methods and text distillation exist and are not standard practice in emulations, and no routine test certifies that a representation encodes prognosis rather than the treatment that was about to be given.
problems.why_open: The causal role of an embedding dimension is not interpretable, so the standard remedy of inspecting an adjustment set does not apply. Predictiveness of treatment is the obvious test and settles nothing: a genuinely prognostic representation predicts treatment through confounding by indication, and a leaking one predicts it directly. Restricting to pre-assignment text bounds the leak without eliminating it, because a note written before treatment can describe a decision already taken, and validity therefore rests on auditable content provenance rather than on timing metadata.
problems.proposed_direction: Use temporally locked encoders trained on content demonstrably prior to both the assignment and the treatment decision, and publish the provenance of that window in dates and document types rather than in prose. Adopt the existing treatment-leakage tests and text distillation methods rather than treating predictiveness as a diagnostic, and where a representation is used as a proxy, state the proximal role and the identification conditions it requires. Prefer interpretable proxy sets over indiscriminate adjustment for a high-dimensional representation whose causal role cannot be argued.

problems.original_statement: Causal forests and meta-learners estimate heterogeneous treatment effects, and they inherit every identification assumption of the base analysis without relaxing any of them. Subgroup discovery adds three specific hazards: confounding that varies by subgroup, multiplicity across the many subgroups a flexible learner implicitly examines, and limited overlap within small strata. Apparent heterogeneity can therefore reflect differential measurement, differential healthcare access or model extrapolation rather than differential biology. The distributional problem is that the groups with the least data and the poorest overlap are frequently the protected groups whose effects the analysis was undertaken to examine, so the least reliable estimates carry the most weight in interpretation.
problems.correction_note: The claim that protected groups have the poorest overlap is an empirical claim about a particular dataset and has to be shown there rather than assumed. Adaptive subgroup selection also needs selection-aware inference specifically, and restricting to regions of adequate overlap changes the target population rather than repairing the estimate.
problems.statement: Causal forests and meta-learners estimate heterogeneous treatment effects and inherit every identification assumption of the base analysis without relaxing any of them. A subgroup analysis therefore requires subgroup-specific assessment of exchangeability, measurement validity, positivity and uncertainty, and apparent heterogeneity can reflect differential measurement or differential access rather than differential biology. Two further requirements are routinely skipped. Adaptively chosen subgroups need selection-aware inference, because the reported interval otherwise conditions on a subgroup the data chose. And restricting to regions with adequate overlap changes the target population rather than fixing the estimate, so it has to be reported as a change of question. Where the groups with the poorest support are the protected groups the analysis was undertaken to examine, that has to be demonstrated in the data at hand rather than assumed, and it is neither demonstrated nor required to be.
problems.why_open: Overlap within a subgroup is a property of the data that no estimator improves, and restricting to where it holds removes the subgroups a fairness analysis exists to report on. Distinguishing effect modification from differential measurement requires validation data within each subgroup, which is scarcest where the subgroup is smallest. Honest sample splitting and selection-aware inference both cost precision in exactly the strata that are already imprecise, so the statistically correct analysis is the one least able to say anything.
problems.proposed_direction: Report subgroup-specific data support, calibration and uncertainty next to every subgroup effect, so a wide and poorly supported estimate cannot be read as a finding, and show the support of protected groups in the data at hand rather than asserting it. Use honest sample splitting and selection-aware inference for adaptively chosen subgroups, and state overlap restriction as a change of target population when it is used. Evaluate not only whether benefit varies across groups but whether the emulation's identification assumptions hold equally across them, since differential measurement and differential access are alternative explanations for the same pattern.
